title: Organic Chemistry
lines: Organic questions reward pattern recognition: spot the functional group, and you know the reactions. Carbon forms four bonds, hydrogen one, oxygen two. Keep that count in mind when checking any formula.
## Alkanes
- General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; saturated, single C–C bonds only. Methane CH₄ is tetrahedral (bond angle 109°28′).
- Stable: no reaction with acidified KMnO₄, bromine water, strong acids or bases.
- Combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
- Substitution with Cl₂ in light: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, continuing to CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. Each step replaces one H and gives one HCl. The products form a mixture.
- Boiling points rise with chain length; for the same formula, more branching means a lower boiling point. C1–C4 alkanes are gases at room temperature.
> Example: How many moles of Cl₂ are needed to convert 1 mol CH₄ completely into CCl₄?
> Each Cl atom that enters replaces one H, and each Cl₂ supplies one Cl to the product (the other forms HCl). Four H replaced, so 4 mol Cl₂.
## Alkenes and alkynes
- Alkenes CₙH₂ₙ contain C=C. Ethene C₂H₄ is planar (bond angles about 120°). Alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ contain C≡C; ethyne C₂H₂ is linear.
- Addition across the multiple bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br (bromine water or Br₂ in CCl₄ is decolourised).
- CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH (catalyst, heat, pressure); CH₂=CH₂ + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl; CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃ (Ni catalyst).

- Alkenes and alkynes are oxidised by acidified KMnO₄ (purple colour fades); ethene is oxidised to CO₂, so KMnO₄ cannot be used to remove ethene from methane (it adds CO₂ impurity). Use bromine water instead.
- Ethene ripens fruit and is the measure of a country's petrochemical industry.
- Ethyne: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂↑. HC≡CH + 2Br₂ → CHBr₂CHBr₂.
! Trap: bromine water decolourised by benzene is extraction (physical), not addition. Only true addition counts as a reaction.
## Benzene
- C₆H₆: planar regular hexagon, all six C–C bonds identical, in between single and double. No ordinary C=C, so it does not decolourise bromine water by reaction or acidified KMnO₄.
- Substitution is easier than addition: C₆H₆ + Br₂ → C₆H₅Br + HBr (FeBr₃ catalyst, liquid bromine); nitration C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O (concentrated H₂SO₄, 50–60 °C).
- Addition only under strong conditions: C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂ (cyclohexane, Ni, heat).
- Methylbenzene (toluene) is oxidised by KMnO₄ (the side chain), unlike benzene.
## Functional groups

- Alcohols –OH: ethanol C₂H₅OH. 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂↑ (gentler than water). Catalytic oxidation: 2CH₃CH₂OH + O₂ → 2CH₃CHO + 2H₂O (Cu or Ag catalyst, heat). Strong oxidants (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, orange to green) take it to acetic acid.
- Aldehydes –CHO: ethanal CH₃CHO. Oxidised to acids; give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent and a brick-red Cu₂O precipitate with fresh Cu(OH)₂ on heating. Reduced by H₂ back to alcohols.
- Carboxylic acids –COOH: acetic acid CH₃COOH, a weak acid stronger than carbonic acid: 2CH₃COOH + CaCO₃ → (CH₃COO)₂Ca + H₂O + CO₂↑ (removes scale).
- Esters –COO–: ethyl acetate CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, fruity smell, less dense than water, insoluble. Hydrolysis is reversible in acid and complete in base.
> Example: Which reagent tells ethanol, acetic acid and ethanal apart in one test?
> Fresh Cu(OH)₂ suspension: acetic acid dissolves it to a blue solution; ethanal gives a brick-red precipitate on heating; ethanol shows no change.
! Memory chain: alkene → alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid → ester. Each arrow is a named reaction: addition of water, oxidation, oxidation, esterification.
## Isomerism

- Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Chain isomers differ in branching; position isomers differ in where the group sits; functional group isomers differ in the group (ethanol C₂H₅OH and dimethyl ether CH₃OCH₃).
- Count of alkane isomers: C₄H₁₀ has 2, C₅H₁₂ has 3, C₆H₁₄ has 5.
- Count monochloro products by counting the different kinds of H (symmetry). n-butane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ has 2 kinds of H, so 2 monochloro products.
- Cis-trans isomers need each C of C=C to carry two different groups (but-2-ene has them; propene does not).
> Example: How many isomers does C₅H₁₂ have and which has only one monochloro product?
> Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane: 3 isomers. In 2,2-dimethylpropane C(CH₃)₄ all 12 H are equivalent, so it gives only one monochloro product.
! Trap: CH₂Cl₂ has no isomers because methane is tetrahedral, not flat. This fact is evidence for the tetrahedral shape.
## Naming simple compounds
- Find the longest carbon chain (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex- for 1 to 6 carbons). Number from the end that gives the substituents (or the functional group) the smallest numbers.
- Write substituents in alphabetical order with numbers; use di-, tri- for repeats: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₃ is 2,3-dimethylbutane.
- For alkenes and alcohols the chain must contain the C=C or the C bearing –OH, numbered to give it the lowest number: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ is but-1-ene; CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ is propan-2-ol.
! Trap: a name like 2-ethylbutane is wrong; the longest chain actually has 5 carbons, giving 3-methylpentane.
## Reaction types
- Substitution: one atom or group replaces another (alkane halogenation, benzene bromination and nitration, esterification, ester hydrolysis).
- Addition: atoms add to both ends of a C=C or C≡C (hydrogenation, bromine addition, hydration).
- Elimination: a small molecule is removed to form a multiple bond: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O (concentrated H₂SO₄, 170 °C). At 140 °C the same mixture gives diethyl ether instead (a substitution).
- Esterification: CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH ⇌ CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O (concentrated H₂SO₄, heat). The acid loses –OH and the alcohol loses H (shown by ¹⁸O labelling: the ¹⁸O of the alcohol ends up in the ester).
- In the lab ester is collected over saturated Na₂CO₃ solution, which removes acid, dissolves alcohol and lowers the ester's solubility.
- Oxidation and reduction in organic chemistry: gaining O or losing H is oxidation; gaining H is reduction.
> Example: 6 g of acetic acid reacts with excess ethanol with a yield of 50 %. What mass of ethyl acetate forms?
> n(acid) = 6/60 = 0.1 mol, so theoretical ester = 0.1 mol × 88 = 8.8 g. At 50 %, 4.4 g.
## Polymerisation
- Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers: n CH₂=CH₂ → –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ– (polyethene). Chloroethene gives PVC; propene gives polypropene; styrene gives polystyrene.
- To find the monomer of an addition polymer, take the two-carbon repeat unit and put back the double bond.
- Condensation polymerisation also releases small molecules (water); examples are polyesters and proteins (from amino acids).
## Basic biomolecules

- Sugars: glucose and fructose C₆H₁₂O₆ (isomers; glucose has an aldehyde group and gives a silver mirror). Sucrose and maltose C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Starch and cellulose (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ are not isomers because n differs. Starch turns iodine blue; its hydrolysis finally gives glucose.
- Fats and oils are esters of glycerol with fatty acids. Oils (liquid) contain more C=C and can be hardened by adding H₂. Hydrolysis in NaOH is saponification and makes soap.

- Proteins are polymers of amino acids (–NH₂ and –COOH groups). They coagulate reversibly with light-metal salts like (NH₄)₂SO₄ (salting out) and irreversibly with heat, heavy-metal ions, strong acids or bases, ethanol or formaldehyde (denaturation). Concentrated HNO₃ turns some proteins yellow; burnt protein smells like burnt feathers.
! Trap: fats, sugars and proteins are not all polymers. Fats and glucose are small molecules; starch, cellulose and proteins are natural polymers.
